original_summary: A man's body is found in a thicket near the mountain road to Yamashina, stabbed once in the chest, and seven people give their accounts to a police magistrate. A woodcutter, who found the body that morning, says there was no sword near it, only a length of rope at the foot of a cedar and a comb, and that the ground was trampled as if there had been a hard fight. A traveling monk saw the man the day before, walking beside a woman on a horse (her face hidden by a veil), the man carrying a sword and a bow with some twenty arrows. A constable says he caught the famous bandit Tajomaru, who had fallen from the dead man's horse and lay groaning on a stone bridge, carrying the dead man's bow and arrows; he adds that Tajomaru is known for chasing women and that the woman on the horse is missing. An old woman says the dead man was her son-in-law Takehiro, a gentle twenty-six-year-old samurai from Wakasa, that her nineteen-year-old daughter Masago is strong-willed and has known no other man, and begs the magistrate to find her daughter. Tajomaru then confesses that he killed the man: he glimpsed the woman's face when the wind lifted her veil, decided to take her even if he had to kill her husband, lured the couple into the thicket with a story of buried treasure, tied the man to a cedar and brought the wife; she drew a small dagger and fought him, but he overpowered her and took her by force; as he turned to leave, she clung to him and cried that one of the two men must die, because she could not bear the shame before both; he untied the husband and fought him fairly, killing him on the twenty-third stroke, but the wife had disappeared. Masago's account, given at Kiyomizu temple, is that after the bandit left she saw in her bound husband's eyes only a cold, contemptuous light, begged him to die with her, took up the dagger and, when his lips silently said 'Kill me', stabbed him in a daze; she then tried again and again to kill herself and failed, and asks what she should do. The dead man's spirit, speaking through a medium, says the bandit comforted the wife and offered to take her; she answered 'Take me anywhere', then pointed at her husband and begged the bandit to kill him; even the bandit was shocked, kicked her down and asked the husband whether to kill her; she ran away, the bandit left, and the man, alone, took up the dagger his wife had dropped and stabbed himself in the chest; then someone crept up to him and an unseen hand quietly drew the dagger out, and he sank for ever into the darkness.
seed_elements: The story is a set of seven separate spoken testimonies about one death in a thicket, with no narrator who knows the truth and no verdict: the first four speakers (a woodcutter, a traveling monk, a constable and an old woman) answer a police magistrate about what they saw and know, and the last three (the bandit Tajomaru, the wife Masago and the dead husband Takehiro) each speak about what happened in the thicket. Nobody says which account is true.

The woodcutter says he found the body that morning in a bamboo and cedar thicket away from the road, stabbed once in the chest, the blood already dry; there was no sword or bow, only a length of rope at the foot of a cedar and a comb, and the ground was trampled as if the man had fought hard before he died; no horse could have come in.

The monk says he met the dead man the day before at about noon, walking with a woman on a horse (her face hidden by a veil, her robes pink-and-green), the man carrying a sword and a bow with many arrows; he never imagined the man would die, and thinks of how short human life is.

The constable says he caught Tajomaru, a famous bandit, groaning beside a stone bridge after falling from a horse, carrying the dead man's bow and arrows; he is sure Tajomaru is the killer, says Tajomaru is a notorious chaser of women, and asks the magistrate to find the woman, who has disappeared.

The old woman says the dead man, Takehiro, a gentle twenty-six-year-old samurai from Wakasa, was her daughter's husband; her daughter Masago, nineteen, is proud and strong-willed and has known no other man; the couple left for Wakasa the day before, and she begs the magistrate to find her daughter and curses the bandit, weeping.

Tajomaru confesses with pride that he killed the man: a breeze lifted the wife's veil and her face seemed to him like a goddess's; he tricked the husband into the thicket with a story of buried treasure and tied him to a cedar, then brought the wife; she drew a dagger and fought like no woman he had known, but he overpowered her; as he turned to go, she clung to him and cried that one of the two men must die, and that she would go with whichever survived; he untied the husband, fought him fairly and killed him on the twenty-third stroke (no one else had lasted twenty), but the wife had vanished, so he took the sword and bow and left.

Masago, giving her account at Kiyomizu temple, says that after the bandit had taken her by force and left, the cold, contemptuous look in her bound husband's eyes hurt her more than the blow; she begged him to die with her, took up the dagger when she could not endure the look, and stabbed him when his lips silently said 'Kill me'; then she tried to drown or stab herself, but could not die, and she asks, weeping, what a woman like her should do.

Takehiro's spirit, speaking through a medium, says the bandit sat down beside his wife and comforted her; he, bound and unable to speak, tried to warn her with his eyes; but she looked up and said 'Take me anywhere', then pointed at him and cried 'Kill that man'; the bandit was shocked, kicked her down and asked him whether to kill her or let her live; she ran into the thicket and the bandit left, cutting one rope; alone, he took up the dagger his wife had dropped and stabbed himself in the chest.

The story ends with the dead man's last words: the thicket falls quiet, someone creeps up to him on soft feet, an unseen hand quietly draws the dagger out of his chest, blood fills his mouth once more, and he sinks for ever into the darkness; nothing is added after it.
discarded_elements: The small physical details in the first four testimonies (the horse's colour and height, the number of arrows, the colour of the robes, the distance from the road, the fly on the wound), if space is needed
The constable's account of Tajomaru's earlier crimes and the old woman's description of her daughter's face, if space is needed
Tajomaru's long argument that powerful people also kill with money and words, and the details of the treasure trick and the sword fight beyond the twenty-third stroke, if space is needed
The medium's frame and the stage directions in brackets (smiles, silences, sobbing), except as the speaker's manner, if space is needed
conversion_plan: Keep the original's frame of seven separate spoken testimonies about one death in a thicket, in the original order (the woodcutter, the monk, the constable, the old woman, Tajomaru, Masago, Takehiro's spirit), the original period (old Japan, a mountain road near Kyoto) and the original's refusal to say what really happened; do not modernize the setting, and do not add a narrator who knows the truth, a detective, a judge's verdict, a new witness, a new piece of evidence or a clear culprit. Write it in natural English at about 400 words as a chain of short testimonies: each witness speaks in the first person ('I') in quoted speech with a plain speech tag that names the speaker (for example '"...," said the woodcutter.'), so that every testimony has its own voice and its own purpose; an outside narrator may only say in a few words who is speaking (for example 'The woodcutter was questioned first.') and never comments on whom to believe; the magistrate's questions are only implied by the answers, so do not write quoted lines for the magistrate. Make each witness sound different through what they care about, not through gimmicks: the woodcutter plain and practical, the monk vague and regretful, the constable eager to blame the bandit, the old woman worried about her daughter, Tajomaru proud and boastful, Masago ashamed and broken, Takehiro bitter and wounded. Use the names Tajomaru, Takehiro and Masago (these three only) and role names for everyone else (the woodcutter, the monk, the constable, the old woman). Preserve the contradiction as the heart of the story: after the four outside witnesses set the scene, all three people who were in the thicket each claim the death for themselves, with their own reasons: Tajomaru says he killed the man fairly in a sword fight, after the woman begged one of the two men to die; Masago says she herself killed her helpless husband with the dagger because of the cold contempt in his eyes; Takehiro says he killed himself with the dagger after his wife asked the bandit to kill him, and that an unseen hand then drew the dagger out of his chest. Keep each of these accounts convincing from the inside, and keep the details that clash (who did what with the dagger, what the wife said and did, how the man died). Do not reconcile the accounts, do not decide which one is true, do not call anyone a liar, and do not write a line that explains the differences. Keep the sexual violence off the page and non-graphic: refer to it with one plain phrase (for example 'he took her by force'), and describe no body or wound in detail. Keep the ending exactly as the original leaves it: it ends on the dead man's last words as he sinks into the darkness, with no verdict, no explanation of who took the dagger, no moral and no comment of your own. Do not reveal in an earlier testimony, in the introductions or anywhere before its turn what a later testimony will say. Compress by trimming the witnesses' small physical details, the bandit's long speeches and the old woman's description of her daughter, and by keeping the first four witnesses brief; do not cut any of the three main accounts, their claims, or the final scene.

title: 藪の中 In a Grove (Ryunosuke Akutagawa)

ending_reveal.meaning: The last testimony, spoken by the dead man's spirit through a medium, says that after the bandit left and his wife fled, he rose from the cedar, took up the small dagger she had dropped and stabbed himself in the chest; the thicket fell silent, then someone crept up to him and an unseen hand quietly drew the dagger out of his chest, and he sank for ever into the darkness. The story ends on that last scene, with no verdict, no word on which of the three accounts is true, and no explanation of who the unseen person was or what really happened.
ending_reveal.source_quote: おれはそれぎり永久に、中有の闇へ沈んでしまった。
ending_reveal.withhold_until_end: Before the last testimony, do not say or hint what the dead man will tell (that he stabbed himself, or that an unseen hand drew the dagger from his chest), and do not preview, in the introductions or anywhere else, what any later testimony will say; never tell the listener who the real killer is or which account is true, never say that the accounts will be settled or explained, and never add a verdict, a solution, a moral or a comment.

key_causality: One man is found dead in a thicket, and seven people speak about it in turn: four outsiders set the scene (no sword found, only a rope and a comb; the man had been travelling with his wife; the bandit Tajomaru was caught with his bow; the wife is missing), and then each of the three people who were there claims the death for himself or herself, for reasons that fit their own pride, shame or bitterness: Tajomaru says he killed the husband fairly after the wife begged one of the two men to die, Masago says she stabbed her helpless husband because of the cold contempt in his eyes, and Takehiro says he killed himself after his wife asked the bandit to kill him; the accounts clash on who did what, and no one, in or out of the story, resolves the clash.
free_to_cut: the witnesses' small physical details (the horse, the arrows, the clothes, the distance from the road), the monk's regrets and the constable's other accusations against Tajomaru, the old woman's description of her daughter, Tajomaru's long arguments and the details of the treasure trick and the sword fight, and the medium's frame; the first four witnesses may be joined and kept very short
source_essentials.narration_voice: The story has no narrator of its own: it is a series of spoken testimonies, each told in the first person ('I') by the person who gives it, in that person's own voice and self-interest; a short, neutral outside narrator may only say who is speaking (for example 'The woodcutter was questioned first.'), never judges, comments or says which account is true, and is never the one who knows what happened; the police magistrate who questions the witnesses stays silent, and the dead man speaks through a medium but in his own first-person voice.
